posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: The attached page is from the first edition of Saxby's "Practical Holography" (from the section on fringe-locking). I've often wondered about this geometry to generate fringes for fringe-locking. It shows how portions of the expanded beams (object and reference) are diverted off to the side to generate fringes. The note at the bottom of the page says "Part of the object illuminating beam is deflected by mirror M to overlap the reference beam at a small angle, generating broad live fringes in the region of overlap." I've never tried to overlap expanded beams at a "small angle" to produce fringes. It seems unlikely at first glance, but evidently it works. I was wondering if anyone has tried it.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello Joe,

That doesn't look good to me at all. Without a mirror or beam splitter in there somewhere to get the angle between those beams much smaller it won't produce visible interference at all. You need visible fringes to get good locking. 

The beams should be pretty much superimposed over each other to get nice fringes for locking. Maybe a few degrees difference to get them a little smaller sometimes, but not much at all. Nothing like that diagram. That looks close to 20 degrees difference between the two beams. 

I bet Bob H could give you more exact information on this. I think he uses a locker on a regular basis. 

I bet you have "overlap expanded beams at a "small angle" to produce fringes" even though you don't realize it. You've made a Michaelson interferometer right? There you go. That's all your really doing with a locker. Taking some of the two beams AFTER they have passed through your actual recording setup, getting them to line up so the fringes are large enough to be visible. From there you can stick the sensors of the locker (there are two of them in that one head) over the bright and dark parts of that interference pattern.

For many setups you need another mirror or beam splitter to get those two beams coming from the same direction. The Saxby illustration is missing that component. 

Jeff W

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks for your comments Jeff. The diagram doesn't really make sense to me either. By the way, the same sketch was repeated in the 2nd edition of Saxby's book. I think the origin of the diagram is from the instruction manual for the Dikrotek fringe-locker, according to Saxby's footnote Even though I don't understand it, I can't help feeling that the arrangement was a workable one (for Rallison) but I'm not "connecting" with the exact manner in which the fringes are generated, either it's my fault or the diagram's. It might have something to do with the mirror which is shown reflecting light from the reference beam.

I agree about using a standard Michelson or Mach-Zehnder interferometer in the setup (by picking off beams and using a beamsplitter to generate fringes). That's what I'm working on now. But this diagram is on my mind, because if it's workable, it has an advantage over the standard method of generating fringes. The reason is because whenever a separate interferometer is incorporated into a setup for fringe-locking, the fringes are not an "exact" replica of the fringes that are being generated in the hologram. By that, I mean that there are some components in the interferometer leg of the setup (posts, mirrors, beamsplitter) that are not part of the same "beam path" for the hologram fringes. So the fringe-locker could be making corrections due to path length changes in the interferometer leg, which do not correspond to changes in the hologram leg. It can be made reasonably close, and that is probably good enough (as mentioned, that's what I'm working on now). But the Rallison diagram has the advantage that the actual beams forming the fringes are being picked off very far downstream, in fact they are all the way downstream, with only a single mirror involved at the end. So it seems a closer approximation of the fringes that are actually being formed in the hologram.

But I do agree that the diagram seems unlikely, I certainly can't figure it out.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello Joe,

Exactly, he had that extra mirror downstream. A beam splitter on a stand will do the same. Either way, your trying to get the beams pretty much overlapped. 

If you can use a simple mirror in your setup that would be better as the locker would have a stronger signal. It all depends on the setup and the coherence of your laser. Mirrors usually take up more coherence than the splitter but both beams need to go through the splitter giving you only half the power at the lockers detectors. 

I wasn't saying to pick off beams and make a Michaelson. I was talking about taking the run off beams after the plate, just like in the diagram, and making THOSE beams over lap just like the final output of a Michaelson. 

On the Saxby diagram all you need is a large beamsplitter, so no small cubes a plate is the way to go. A 50/50 would be best. If you don't have one just try a regular piece of glass but make it thick so your not looking at the fringes created by the first and second surface. 

Take the beam splitter and put it right where the two beams cross after the object and plate have been passed already. Right near where the diagram shows the fringes. Set the beam splitter so the beam lighting up the object is now on the same path as the beam lighting up the H1.

The beam splitter would be tilted like a forward slash /, tilting from 1 oclock to 7 oclock in this diagram. It would bend the object beam towards the left as it progresses downstream. Now the two beams are right on top of each other going the same way. Visible fringes. 

You could also do it the other way. Have the splitter leaning like a back slash \. That way the H1 beam would now be following the same path as the object beam. Some setups it easier one way or the other. 

Jeff Weil

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: Thanks Jeff, I think I've got it now, with your help. The idea is just to get a mirror or beamsplitter in the overspill of object and reference beams, and tweak the angle until the beams overlap (come from the same direction) and generate fringes. It's an interesting idea, and worth keeping in mind, I think. I'm not sure if it will work in my setup, because the reference beam (combined 532/633) is weak due to limited power at 633. Rallison was probably using an ion laser with lots of power to spare. I don't know if I can afford to have an oversized reference beam to allow for placement of the beamsplitter or mirror. I should probably just try it, to see how strong the fringes are, and how much light is wasted. The HeNe light is very precious however.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello Joe,

If you have a combined beam you don't need to read both freq's with the locker. In fact it would be better to lose one of them anyway. You really want only one set of fringes in the lockers sensors or you'll get something similar to cross talk between them. 

If the beam is combined then it's going through many of the same optics. Locking the fringes of only one freq will remove the motion problems for those optics no matter how many frequencies are hitting it.

Jeff W

No need to get rid of the overspill method. Just use a dicro mirror or beam splitter that only reflects one freq, or use a filter to get rid of one of the colors. 

Jeff Weil

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: That illustration is completely useless. You'd need a beamsplitter where the two beams overlap to get them nearly collinear to get fringes to lock. The fringe locker also wouldn't see the object or the plateholder, and the fringe locker's additional beamsplitter must be the most stable component on the table to avoid it from making everything worse. Fringe lockers are very difficult to use in pictorial set-ups, especially with more than one object beam. Not worth the hassle.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello BobH,

I totally agree. I could see them being used as some diagnostic device, or to lock two lasers together of course, but not for display holography. 

I have a nice one and messed with it once or twice but never seriously thought of using it for a real job. 

There's just no substitute for a stable table and setup.

Jeff W

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Thanks Bob. I do want to give fringe-locking a fair shake, and see what happens. I'm going to have some separate fringes on the table in any event, so it's a fairly minor thing to add my homemade fringe-locker.

My table room is a sealed room enclosed with 2-inch styrofoam for the walls and ceiling. I used a Mach-Zehnder interferometer to check the stability of the table. (I was on the other side of the styrofoam room with the lasers, watching the fringes on a video monitor.) The fringes do eventually come to a dead halt (no movement whatever over 2 hours) but it took 4 hours. The laser was warming the area on the outside of the styrofoam room, so I think this was the main factor. It probably took the 4 hours to reach some kind of thermal equilibrium. I've done plenty of monochrome Denisyuk DCG holograms here, but the exposure times were relatively short, in the 30 second range, with 200mW at 457nm. So there was no need for ultra-stability, and hardly any warm-up time was required.

But with dye-sensitized DCG and long exposure times, on the order of 5 to 10 minutes, thing are obviously going to be a lot different, those additional fringes are going to be essential to get an idea of the table's thermal stability. Split-beam MBDCG with a HeNe is proving to be quite difficult. The idea of using the fringe-locker is to reduce settling times, because when I'm moving about in the table room (changing plates, etc.) I will be disturbing the equilbrium, and I don't know how long it will take for things to settle down (thus the need for separate fringes for monitoring). Actually I would much prefer not to use the fringe-locker, but I will have to see what the actual settling times are.

By the way, Bob, I'm using the achromatic 1/2 waveplate, the broadband cube beamsplitter, and the achromatic polarization rotator. They are all working well. I'm very glad you suggested moving away from a metallized beamsplitter. With so many optics on the table, the losses from a metallized beamsplitter would have been unacceptable. The polarization rotator film appears to have de-laminated inside the glass sandwich in some areas, but there is an unaffected area where it's still adhering to the glass, so I'm careful to direct the beam through that area.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
I have three at work that I use for everything, but all HOEs. They could work well in a stereogram set-up too, because everything stays constant after it's all made to work. Use on a transfer set-up is practical too, for the same reason. The geometry is pretty well fixed, so the fringe locking system can be implemented easily. Takes out all table expansion, air current drift, and vibration of most of the components (don't really need to float the table with it!). Have to be careful about adjusting the fringes for locking, to avoid making the fringes move more because of the device itself. It's a skill that needs to be practiced.

Sorry to hear about the de-lamination Joe. Maybe pry it apart and re-glue? I used Norland 61. I can send a replacement if you'd like, or replacement windows.

posts.content_md:
I read the photo as good but the caption is wrong. To me it looks like the object beam is reflecting of the M and crossing back across the object beam by close to 90 degrees. This intersection of Object to Reference at 90 degrees is very suitable. Just place a BS where he shows the fringe spot at (the small black dot), redirect this to a lens and you should be able to see real time fringes or lock them. Not sure why you want to lock two beams in a SBR hologram anyway. Your not actually seeing the object beam off the object. It will indicate if studied while exposing if the laser freaked out, but even if one of those beams moved in a SBR, you would still get a hologram if the object itself did not move with relation to the plate.

I did use a similar technique a few time to monitor real time fringes during a split beam shot.

Rallison wrote something (shown below) which seems to explain the diagram I posted earlier. But that diagram must be in error (which now seems clear, thanks to everyone's help). Basically the diagram is OK, except that a beamsplitter and lens need to be inserted, just as John has shown above. All that's happening is that a beamsplitter is being inserted into the overspill, in some area where the object beam and reference beam intersect, and the beamsplitter is tilted until the the beams overlap (i.e., are co-linear and going in the same direction) and the lens provides the expansion to get visible fringes.

This layout might have a few disadvantages. First, the beamsplitter really should have some phsyical connection both to the object and plateholder, which will take some advance planning. Secondly, I'm not sure what a diffuse object beam will do. My guess is that a diffuse beam (having going through a diffusion screen) will not produce fringes (?) Also, a fair amount of expansion will be needed for the reference beam to get enough overspill, which will be wasteful of light.

posts.author: Johnfp
posts.content_md:
Hey Joe, there are many disadvantages as well as advantages to fringe locking. The biggest draw back is if your holographic system is nice and stable and you put a fringe locker in and any of the optics inserted in the system exclusively for fringe locking moves, then the locker actually destroys your hologram by purposely introducing movement into the tranducer mirror. Also, it's almost impossible to get the fringe locker to acually be the beam coming off the object and the beam being reflected off the plate to insure those two are stable also. Usually fringe locking is done just after the spatial filters which in itself are expanding beams, thus to set up an "interferometer" while catching those lights, proves to be tricky.

Not to sound to negative on Fringe Locking, but I have found that just insuring my set up is stable is enough and forget about the fringe locker. Just my opinion.
